info.name: Private Cloud Control Plane — Phase 6 (minikube)
info.description:
Exercises the control plane running on the minikube cluster, through the Gateway, in lifecycle order.

**Run the `00 Identity` folder first.** It mints the bearer tokens every other request carries, from the in-cluster OIDC fixture reached over a port-forward:

```bash
kubectl port-forward -n private-cloud svc/local-oidc 18085:18080
```

Then run the whole collection top to bottom. Requests that expect a refusal — a 403 for a foreign project, a 409 for a purge inside the retention window — assert the refusal: those are safety rules, and a run in which they stopped failing would be a regression.

Generated from `tools/postman/requests.mjs`; do not hand-edit. Regenerate with `node tools/postman/generate-collection.mjs`.

item.name: 00 Identity
item.description: Mints the bearer tokens every later request carries. The issuer is the in-cluster OIDC fixture, reached over a `kubectl port-forward`; it has no route through the Gateway and is not meant to have one. Run this folder first: every other folder reads the variables it sets.

request.description: A `tenant_developer` in the seeded project. Valid for 15 minutes — re-run this request rather than debugging a sudden 401.
A `platform_administrator`. Administrative recovery is never inferred from project membership, so this role is checked on its own and the two tokens are not interchangeable in either direction.
A correctly signed token for a project the caller does not belong to. Used later to prove that a valid signature is not by itself authorisation.

item.name: 01 Health and routing
item.description: The unauthenticated probes, and the one header that decides which environment answers. `X-Canary: green` reaches the preview Service; everything else reaches the active one.

request.description: Deliberately unauthenticated: a liveness probe that needs a token cannot run from a kubelet.
Readiness is the gate the blue-green promotion waits on. A green ReplicaSet whose pods never report ready is aborted by the progress deadline rather than promoted.

Same path, same Gateway, different backend. Gateway API resolves the tie by header match count, so the rule carrying `X-Canary: green` wins over the one that matches everything. When no rollout is in progress the preview Service points at the same ReplicaSet as the active one, so this answers identically — that is correct, not a routing failure.

item.name: 02 Project, quota, and catalog
item.description: The read surface a caller needs before it can compose a valid create request.

exec: pm.test('limits and usage are both reported', () => { const q = pm.response.json(); pm.expect(q).to.have.property('limits'); pm.expect(q).to.have.property('usage'); });

request.description: `usage` is measured, not cached: it is computed inside the same read that returns it, so a create accepted a moment ago is already counted.

item.name: 03 Create an instance
item.description: The asynchronous accept path, and the two behaviours that make it safe to retry. A create returns 202 with an operation to follow; it does not return an instance, because no instance exists yet.

exec: // A fresh key per run. Reusing one would replay the stored response from a previous run
// and this request would stop testing anything.
// A hostname unique to this run, so repeated runs do not collide on a name.
pm.test('is not reported as a replay', () => pm.expect(accepted.replayed).to.eql(false));

request.description: The `Idempotency-Key` header is required. The response carries `operationId`, `targetId` (the new instance), and a `statusUrl` to poll. The instance is not usable until that operation reaches `succeeded`.

item.name: Create instance again with the same key (replay)

exec: // Deliberately the *same* key as "createKey", to exercise the replay path.
pm.test('is reported as a replay', () => pm.expect(replay.replayed).to.eql(true));
pm.test('returns the original operation, not a new one', () => pm.expect(replay.operationId).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('operationId')));

request.description: The same key with the same payload returns the *stored* response. This is the behaviour that makes a client retry safe: a second VM is never built, and the caller is handed back the operation it already started.

item.name: Create instance with the same key but a different payload

exec: // Deliberately the *same* key as "createKey", to exercise the replay path.

request.description: A reused key with different content is a client bug, not a retry, and is refused. The payload is compared by canonical hash, so key order and whitespace do not matter and a genuinely identical body still replays.

item.name: Poll the create operation until it settles

exec: // Re-sends itself until 'state' settles, up to 60 attempts.
// An error response will never settle, so it ends the poll immediately. Without this a
// mistyped id polls a 400 until the attempt cap, and a two-second bug takes four minutes

request.description: Re-sends itself until the operation leaves `pending`/`running`. In the Postman GUI this uses `postman.setNextRequest`, so it works in a collection run; sending it once by hand simply shows the current state.

The operation journal for the project. Every accepted command appears here whether it succeeded, failed, or is still running, which makes it the place to look when a caller lost the `operationId` a 202 returned.

item.name: 06 Retention and purge
item.description: `DELETE` on an instance does not delete it. It detaches access and retains the resource, and only an administrator can destroy what is left — after the retention window has expired. The refusal in the last request is the safety rule working, not a failure.

request.description: The VM keeps existing. Access is detached, the address is quarantined rather than reissued, and a retention deadline is stamped from the policy.

// mistyped id polls a 400 until the attempt cap, and a two-second bug takes four minutes

item.name: Confirm the instance is retained, not gone

exec: pm.test('reports when it stops being recoverable', () => pm.expect(retained.retentionDeadline).to.not.eql(null));

item.name: Purge is refused inside the retention window

exec: pm.test('is refused as busy, not accepted', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().code).to.eql('INSTANCE_BUSY'));

request.description: The default policy retains for 168 hours, so a purge moments after a retain is refused. Making this succeed on purpose is a lab-only step documented in the operations manual; there is no API that shortens the window today.

The caller must name the instance twice, in the path and in the body, and the two must agree. A purge is the one irreversible operation in the API, so the request has to be unambiguous about what it is destroying.

item.name: 07 Administration
item.description: The administrative surface that is served today. Each requires `platform_administrator`; project membership grants none of it.

item.name: Get an operation as an administrator

request.description: The same operation the tenant route returns, without requiring the administrator to be a member of the project that owns it.

exec: pm.test('records the action that actually happened', () => pm.expect(audit.items.some((entry) => entry.action === 'retain_instance' && entry.outcome === 'succeeded')).to.eql(true));

request.description: Every accepted command writes an audit entry in the same transaction that accepts it, so this list cannot disagree with what actually happened. The second assertion guards a real defect: every terminal entry was once labelled `create_instance` regardless of the capability that produced it, so the log claimed a VM had been built once per power change, resize, snapshot, and retention.
Empty on a healthy run. Raw poison-record bytes are never stored or returned here — the entry carries identifiers and a classification, not the payload that broke.
Reconciliation observes and reports. It never repairs by deleting or stopping anything; a disagreement it cannot explain becomes a manual review, not an action.

exec: // Nothing to act on. Skipping is the correct outcome, not a silent pass.

request.description: Skipped when the previous request found no dead letters, which is the normal case. A replay is authorised in one transaction and admitted back only after a three-way check on generation, payload hash, and the outbox row that authorised it.

item.name: 08 Authorization and validation
item.description: The refusals. Each of these is a rule the control plane is supposed to enforce, so each asserts the refusal rather than tolerating a range.

item.name: A token for another project is rejected

request.description: The signature is valid and the role is right. Membership is what is missing, and it is checked in the application layer so REST and gRPC get the rule from one place.

item.name: A tenant token cannot reach the admin surface
A malformed create body is rejected

request.description: Missing `flavorId` and `networkId`. Rejected by the transport before any transaction opens, so nothing is written and no operation is created.

item.name: A create without an Idempotency-Key is rejected

request.description: The header is required on every mutating call. Without it a client retry after a timeout could not be distinguished from a second request, which is how duplicate VMs get built.

item.name: 09 Declared but not yet served
item.description: These operations are in the OpenAPI document and in the generated clients, and the control-api has no route for them yet. They answer 404 today. They are kept in the collection deliberately: when a later phase implements one, this folder is where the change shows up, and until then the collection states the gap instead of hiding it. See the coverage table in the API examples document.
